knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4)

```{r setup}
library(bayesSampleMix)
```

## Model and algorithm

The target model is $y = x'\beta + \varepsilon$, $\varepsilon \sim
N(0,\sigma^2)$, with priors $\beta \sim N(0, 25 I)$ and $\sigma^2 \sim
IG(2, 1)$ (see `?mixture_prior`). All full conditionals are conjugate, so the
sampler is a pure Gibbs sampler:

1. $z_j \mid \cdot$ — Bernoulli, from the ratio of the two component
   densities;
2. $\pi \mid z$ — Beta;
3. $\beta, \sigma^2 \mid \cdot$ — normal / inverse-gamma given the P sample and
   the NP units with $z_j = 1$;
4. contaminating component — $\mu_0, \tau^2$ (M0, Mjoint) or a rival
   regression $\beta_{bad}, \sigma^2_{bad}$ (M1).

## Data with 50% severe contamination

Half of the NP units have covariates centred at 10 (far outside the P
support) and outcomes around $-50$, unrelated to the target regression
$y = 2 + 5x$.

```{r data}
d <- simulate_mixture_data("gaussian", n_prob = 100, n_nonprob = 200,
                           contamination = 0.5, beta = c(2, 5),
                           bad_beta = c(-50, 0), x_shift = 10, seed = 123)
plot(y ~ x1, data = d$nonprob, col = ifelse(contaminated == 1, "firebrick", "grey40"),
     pch = 19, cex = 0.6, main = "NP sample (red = contaminated)")
points(y ~ x1, data = d$prob, col = "steelblue", pch = 3, cex = 0.6)
```

```{r fits}
fits <- lapply(c(M0 = "M0", Mjoint = "Mjoint", M1 = "M1"), function(m)
  mixture_fit(y ~ x1, d$prob, d$nonprob, model = m,
              n_iter = 2000, burnin = 1000, seed = 1))
pooled <- baseline_fit(y ~ x1, rbind(d$prob, d$nonprob[names(d$prob)]),
                       n_iter = 2000, burnin = 1000, seed = 1)
rbind(truth = c(2, 5), naive_pooled = coef(pooled), t(sapply(fits, coef)))
sapply(fits, contamination)
```

With such strong separation all three variants identify the contaminated
units; naive pooling produces a meaningless fit. (`M0` and `Mjoint` even give
identical draws here: the outcomes alone classify every unit with probability
0 or 1 to machine precision, so with the same seed both chains make exactly
the same allocations.)

```{r scores}
s <- filter_scores(fits$Mjoint)
range(s[d$nonprob$contaminated == 1])
range(s[d$nonprob$contaminated == 0])
plot(fits$Mjoint, type = "contamination")
```

The posterior of $1-\pi$ is centred near 0.5 but has genuine spread: it is a
population-level parameter. The fraction of the *observed* NP units that are
contaminated is reported separately:

```{r realized}
summary(fits$Mjoint)$contamination
```

## When does the covariate term matter?

`Mjoint` adds information from the covariates. When contaminated units differ
only moderately in their outcomes but lie away from the P covariate
distribution, the leverage term sharpens classification. Compare filter-score
AUCs on a harder design, in which the contaminating regression
$y = 4 + 3x$ crosses the target line $y = 2 + 5x$ at $x = 1$, inside the
region where contaminated covariates are concentrated:

```{r leverage}
d2 <- simulate_mixture_data("gaussian", n_prob = 150, n_nonprob = 300,
                            contamination = 0.3, beta = c(2, 5),
                            bad_beta = c(4, 3), x_shift = 2, seed = 7)
f0 <- mixture_fit(y ~ x1, d2$prob, d2$nonprob, model = "M0",
                  n_iter = 2000, burnin = 1000, seed = 1)
fj <- mixture_fit(y ~ x1, d2$prob, d2$nonprob, model = "Mjoint",
                  n_iter = 2000, burnin = 1000, seed = 1)
labels <- 1 - d2$nonprob$contaminated
c(M0 = filter_auc(labels, filter_scores(f0)),
  Mjoint = filter_auc(labels, filter_scores(fj)))
rbind(truth = c(2, 5), M0 = coef(f0), Mjoint = coef(fj))
```

The covariate term improves both classification and the coefficient
estimates, but some bias remains: contaminated units close to the crossing
point are genuinely indistinguishable from compatible ones. No filter can
remove contamination that is observationally equivalent to the target model
— which is also why such units do little harm.

## Settings worth knowing

* `mixture_control(c_infl = )` controls how much more dispersed contaminated
  covariates are assumed to be (default 4 for the Gaussian family).
* `mixture_prior(pi_shape1, pi_shape2)` encodes prior beliefs about the NP
  sample's reliability.
* For model `"M1"`, `mixture_control(m1_update = "original")` reproduces the
  original research code, which ignored the units allocated to the rival
  regression when there were at most $p + 1$ of them; the default `"exact"`
  uses the correct full conditional.
* Posterior draws for further analysis: `as.matrix(fit, "all")`, e.g.
  `coda::mcmc(as.matrix(fit))`.
